In modern societies, clocks set the hours at which people work and sleep \citep{hamermesh2008cues}. Daylight saving time (DST) relies on this to move an hour of light from the morning to the evening. Whether to keep moving the clock is an open question in many countries. In the United States, the Senate passed a bill making DST permanent in 2022 and the House of Representatives passed another in 2026, which awaits the Senate \citep{uscongress2022sunshine, uscongress2026sunshine}; the European Parliament voted in 2019 to end seasonal clock changes and allow each member state to choose a permanent time regime, a proposal still awaiting the Council \citep{europarl2019seasonal}; Mexico abolished DST in 2022 \citep{mexico2022ley}. Brazil, which had moved its clocks every summer since 1985, abolished DST in April 2019 \citep{brasil2019decreto}. Since then, from November to February, the sun has set an hour earlier on the clock in the states where 131 million Brazilians live \citep{ibge2023censo}. The national grid operator has since studied bringing it back \citep{ons2024nota}. While the debate, in Brazil and elsewhere, has largely focused on electricity \citep{kellogg2008daylight, kotchen2011does}, clock time also determines whether the evening commute occurs in daylight or after dark. The stakes on the road are potentially large: crashes killed 37,150 people in Brazil in 2024, 15 percent of them pedestrians \citep{datasus2025sim}, and road traffic kills about 1.19 million people a year worldwide \citep{who2023global}. % national_road_deaths.rds (13_design_descriptives.R): 2024, 37,150 deaths, 15.3 percent pedestrians.

The choice between permanent time regimes matters because daily activities are coordinated: work and leisure are worth more when they coincide with other people's schedules \citep{hamermesh2008cues}. A clock rule therefore shifts society's entire day relative to daylight at once. Three forces then set its cost on the road. First, people respond to known hazards by reducing their exposure, so observed harm reflects these avoidance responses \citep{neidell2009information}. On the road, avoidance may involve shifting travel away from hours that have become dark. Second, schedules respond to the clock: under DST, people appear to move some activities earlier in the day \citep{sexton2014behavioral}. Third, drivers do not fully internalize the risks their driving imposes on others \citep{edlin2006accident}, including pedestrians and cyclists \citep{crandall1984automobile, white2004arms}. Although avoidance may limit the increase in deaths from darker evenings, drivers' failure to account for the risks they inflict on others may result in less avoidance than is socially optimal. These mechanisms do not establish the net effect on road deaths after travel patterns adjust, including whether brighter mornings offset the additional deaths caused by darker evenings. The evidence on DST and road safety comes mostly from the clock changes themselves, comparing crashes in the days or weeks just before the clocks move with those just after \citep{sullivan2002role, sood2007short, smith2016spring, laliotis2023summertime, gillmore2025daylight}. A clock change shifts daylight relative to clock time overnight. Because work and school schedules remain largely unchanged, comparisons around the transition capture the effect of light before travel patterns have had time to adjust. Each change also adds a second shock, a night with an hour more or less of sleep. Studying a change in the time regime over several seasons avoids both limitations: there is no one-night sleep shock, and travel patterns have time to adjust.

This paper uses Brazil's abolition of DST to estimate how many deaths remain once travel has adjusted and whether brighter mornings offset those deaths. Because DST advanced the clock by one hour, each municipality has, on each summer day, one clock hour in the evening that went from daylight to darkness. It is the hour after sunset in standard time, which was the last hour of sunlight under DST and has been the first hour after sunset since abolition. We compute that hour from the solar position at each municipal seat on each date, and do the same for the hour after standard-time sunrise, which went the other way, from darkness to daylight. We use a triple-difference design that compares the 11 states observing DST in every southern-hemisphere summer from 2008/09 to 2018/19 with 12 states that did not. The estimate contrasts changes before and after abolition in the gap between the summer window and April--August, focusing on the hour that turned dark. Because the affected hour follows local sunset across municipalities and dates, a confounding regional trend would need to align with this shifting hour to explain the estimate. The hours immediately before and after experienced smaller changes in ambient light, from full sun to low sun or from twilight to night, and therefore provide a further check on whether the response follows the change in light. A second design uses every clock hour of the day, each weighted by how much abolition changed its light, computed from the position of the sun. With a separate effect for each clock hour on each date, it tests whether the deaths follow the sun or the clock, and it counts the net change over the day without selecting particular hours.

Two independent high-quality sources measure the outcome. The Ministry of Health's Mortality Information System (SIM) provides death certificates covering fatalities on all public roads in the country. For deaths at the crash scene, the recorded time of death closely approximates the time of the crash. The publicly available crash records of the Federal Highway Police (PRF) cover every crash its officers respond to on federal highways, together with the light conditions the officers recorded at the crash scene. These records show that the evening hour did turn dark: after abolition, the share of crashes in that hour recorded as occurring at dusk or at night rose by 24 percentage points.

We estimate that, after abolition, road deaths in the hour that turned dark rose by 29.2 log points (34 percent), from an average of 110 per summer in the 11 treated states. Deaths and injury crashes on federal highways rose by 54 and 22 log points (71 and 25 percent). Each estimate remains significant under three forms of inference that do not rely on asymptotics with 23 clusters: a score wild bootstrap of the Poisson model, a wild cluster bootstrap of its linear analogue, and a permutation of the treated states. The effect follows the local sun rather than the clock. With clock-hour-by-date fixed effects, we estimate a 48-log-point increase in road deaths when an evening hour shifts from full daylight to night. The estimate remains similar when identification relies only on differences in sunset times across treated states and summer dates.

For road deaths, the season-by-season estimates before abolition show no differential trend. Without the pandemic months the estimate is 23 log points; in the summer window alone, without the off-season comparison, it is 34 and stable across the five seasons without DST. An imputation estimator that extrapolates the pre-abolition trend yields a similar point estimate, although with substantially less precision. The result is also robust to excluding any single state or season. On federal highways, injury crashes show a trend before abolition, and both federal highway estimates shrink once a trend is allowed. We therefore take the magnitude of the effect from road deaths. We use federal highway records to verify the change in light and to investigate the underlying mechanisms. For crashes per vehicle, we focus on seasons without a pre-trend; for pedestrian deaths relative to other road users, we extrapolate the pre-abolition trend. The rise is concentrated in the hour that turned dark and the next one, which went from twilight to night. Road deaths at midday and at night, whose light did not change and where an effect of sleep would also appear, do not rise.

Pedestrians bear a disproportionate share of the increase in deaths. They were 12 percent of road deaths in the hour that turned dark before abolition and account for 43 percent of the excess after it. Their deaths in that hour more than doubled, a rise of 77 log points (115 percent), compared with 18 log points (20 percent) for all other road users. Travel responded to light as well. Hourly counts at the federal highway stations of the National Traffic Count Plan show that traffic in the hour that turned dark fell by about 6 percent and traffic in the morning hour that turned light rose by about 12 percent. Under permutation inference, the first change is borderline and the second is not significant. Over the summers covered by the traffic counts, the risk of an injury crash per vehicle in the hour that turned dark rose by 24 log points (27 percent), more than crashes themselves.

Road deaths in the hour after sunrise, which turned light, show no detectable change ($-3$ log points, standard error 12). When every hour of the day is weighted by how much its light changed, and hours that remained in full daylight or full darkness are assumed unaffected, abolition added 62 road deaths per summer window, from November 15 to February 14 (standard error 12; permutation $p=0.001$). This is the count most directly supported by the observed summer window. Extended to the full DST season, the estimate is 74 deaths (standard error 14). These counts include only deaths at the crash scene with a recorded time; scaling them to deaths without a recorded time and to deaths off the road, most of them in hospitals, raises the summer-window count to between 77 and 157. Estimated over the whole day without assuming which hours were affected, the change is too imprecise (standard error 66) to confirm the count or rule it out. In the model that weights each hour by its change in light, a given change in darkness has a larger effect on road deaths in the evening than in the morning (permutation $p=0.001$).

At a value of a statistical life adjusted to Brazil's income level \citep{robinson2019valuing}, the deaths in one summer window have an estimated cost of 114 million 2025 international dollars,\footnote{An international dollar has the purchasing power that a US dollar has in the United States.} rising to 287 million under the broadest scaling. On the other side of the ledger, the Ministry of Mines and Energy had concluded before abolition that DST no longer saved electricity, possibly because patterns of electricity consumption had changed, particularly through increased late-night air-conditioning demand \citep{mme2019nota}.

The clock changes before 2019 show the same change of light before travel had time to adjust: for three weeks after each change, the evening hour was dark (after February) or light (after October) while travel kept to the same clock hours. Read as the effect of a darker evening, the changes give 42 log points (standard error 14) and abolition 29. The estimate over the whole window, however, averages weeks in which the effect differs. Abolition raised road deaths in hour 0 by 58 log points (13) from mid-November to early December and by 49 (16) in the second half of January, but left no detectable change from Christmas to mid-January (December 24 to January 15). The weeks after the clock changes fall while schools are in session, as do the weeks from mid-November to early December, and in those weeks the effect of abolition is statistically indistinguishable from the effect at the clock changes. This holds both when hour 0 is compared across states and when it is compared with other hours of the same day, a specification that absorbs shocks common to all hours of a day, including the sleep effects of the clock changes. We find no sign that, five summers after abolition, the effect of a darker evening had faded as travel adjusted, although the comparison cannot rule out a moderate decline.

The paper contributes to three literatures. The first estimates the effect of DST on road safety, mostly from the clock changes: in the United States \citep{sood2007short, smith2016spring}, Australia \citep{james2023let}, Greece \citep{laliotis2023summertime}, Chile \citep{gillmore2025daylight}, Brazil \citep{franco2023daylight}, and Mexico \citep{goodwin2024impact}. These studies attribute the deaths that follow the spring change to lost sleep \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight}, and find that the light DST adds to the evening lowers serious crashes \citep{laliotis2023summertime, gillmore2025daylight} or mainly moves deaths between hours of the day \citep{smith2016spring}. Even \citet{depalo2023should}, who explicitly asks whether DST should be abolished, relies on clock transitions to answer that question. Closest to the question of regimes, \citet{bunnings2021spring} estimate the effect of darkness on crashes in Great Britain from the variation in sunrise and sunset times across places and dates, and simulate that year-round DST would save 8 percent of the cost of darkness. \citet{coate2004effects} estimate that year-round DST would avoid 171 pedestrian deaths a year in the United States, and \citet{ferguson1995daylight} that it would have avoided about 900 fatal crashes in 1987--1991, four fifths of them involving pedestrians. \citet{james2023let} also uses the trials of DST in Australian states and its extension for the Sydney Olympics, and finds no long-run effect on road deaths, only a reallocation of crashes across the hours of the day. This paper observes a national change of regime, neither simulated nor temporary, over five seasons and with a first stage recorded by third parties, and compares it with the same change of light at the clock changes, before travel adjusted. It also locates the deaths in the evening hour and among pedestrians, the road users whose crash risk is most sensitive to ambient light \citep{sullivan2002role, woods2025daylight}, even to the brightness of the moon \citep{tyndall2025road}.

The second literature uses DST to identify the effect of ambient light on behavior, mostly crime \citep{doleac2015under, tealde2022unequal, dominguez2023crime}; in Brazil, homicides by firearm fell during the months of DST, mostly in the early-evening hours that DST lit \citep{toro2016daylight}. These studies, like this one, look for the effect in the hours whose light the clock moves. Here the shift of light is permanent, and it arrives without the change in sleep that a clock change brings. Russia's reforms of time-zone boundaries over four decades also shifted light persistently: the daylight regime had a lasting effect on women's sense of safety and an immediate one on the time people spent walking for transport \citep{jelnov2027sunset}.

The third literature weighs the costs and benefits of DST. It has mostly measured energy use \citep{kellogg2008daylight, kotchen2011does} and, through sleep, health and productivity \citep{gibson2018time, giuntella2019sunset, jin2020sleep, osbornechristenson2022saving, jagnani2024children}. The road-safety studies above mostly measure the transitions, which a choice between permanent regimes removes either way. This paper adds the road deaths of the regime itself.

Relative to these literatures, the paper makes the following contributions. First, it estimates the road-safety consequences of an actual change in clock regime, observed over five summers, rather than inferring them from short windows around clock transitions or from simulations. Second, because the hour that turned dark is set by the local sun, the design separates the effect of light from the effects of the clock and of sleep, and it shows that the evening hour that lost light became deadlier while the morning hour that gained light did not become detectably safer. Third, it values the additional road deaths and compares their cost with the energy estimates at the center of Brazil's DST policy debate.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} describes Brazil's DST and its abolition, Section~\ref{sec:data} the data and Section~\ref{sec:design} the design. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the results and Section~\ref{sec:cost} their cost. Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Daylight Saving Time in Brazil and Its Abolition}\label{sec:background}

\subsection{The policy}

Brazil observed DST every summer from 1985/86 to 2018/19. The states covered changed often in the 1990s; from 2008 a standing decree fixed both the dates and the states \citep{brasil2008decreto}. Clocks moved forward at midnight on the third Sunday of October (from 2018, the first Sunday of November; \citealp{brasil2017decreto}) and back on the third Sunday of February, a week later when that Sunday was Carnival Sunday. DST applied in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paran\'a, S\~ao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Esp\'irito Santo, Minas Gerais, Goi\'as, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, and the Federal District, which held 131 million of Brazil's 203 million people in 2022 \citep{ibge2023censo}. Within the sample, Bahia had DST only in 2011/12 and Tocantins only in 2012/13. The North and the rest of the Northeast, close to the equator, where the length of the day varies little over the year, did not have DST in this period. Figure~\ref{fig:map} maps the groups.

Decree 9,772 of April 25, 2019, abolished DST in the whole country \citep{brasil2019decreto}. It followed a technical note of the Ministry of Mines and Energy that concluded that DST had stopped delivering the electricity savings it was designed for \citep{mme2019nota}. By the ministry's estimate, the 2018/19 season had raised electricity load by about 0.7 percent: savings on evening lighting were outweighed by higher consumption late at night, which the note attributed tentatively to air-conditioning. In 2024 the national grid operator estimated that reinstating DST would lower the evening peak, which distributed solar generation has made the binding constraint on the system, and save 96 to 139 million international dollars (R\$244 to 356 million) in thermal-generation fuel in one summer \citep{ons2024nota}.

\subsection{What abolition changed}

DST adds no light to the day; it moves the clock. Panel A of Figure~\ref{fig:light} shows the clock time of sunset and sunrise in S\~ao Paulo over 2018/19, under the DST then in force and without it. In mid-January the sun set at 7:58 p.m.\ on the clock under DST and now sets at 6:58 p.m.; it rose at 6:32 a.m.\ and now rises at 5:32 a.m. % São Paulo, January 15, NOAA equations (EXPLICANDO_O_PROJETO.md, section 1.2).
Because work, school, and the commute keep to the clock, abolition put the people who used to travel in the last hour of sunlight on the road after sunset.

Let $s_{md}$ be the clock time of sunset in standard time at municipality $m$ on day $d$. Under DST the clock ran an hour ahead, so the sun set at clock time $s_{md}+60$ minutes and was above the horizon throughout the clock hour $[s_{md}, s_{md}+60)$. Since abolition the sun has been below the horizon throughout that hour. We call it hour 0, or the hour that turned dark. Its morning counterpart, the clock hour $[r_{md}, r_{md}+60)$ after standard-time sunrise $r_{md}$, was dark under DST and is light now. The neighboring hours changed less: the hour before $s_{md}$ went from full sun to low sun, and the hour after $s_{md}+60$ from twilight to night.

\section{Data}\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Deaths on the road}

The Mortality Information System (Sistema de Informa\c{c}\~oes sobre Mortalidade, SIM) of the Ministry of Health holds every death certificate issued in Brazil, with the underlying cause of death coded in the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision (ICD-10), the municipality and type of place of occurrence, and the date and clock time of death \citep{datasus2025sim}. We select deaths from land-transport crashes (codes V01--V89) that occurred on a public road and call them road deaths. For a person who dies at the crash scene, the time of death is close to the time of the crash: when a federal highway crash with one death and a single road-death certificate fall in the same municipality and day, the certificate's time lies within the hour after the crash in 59 percent of the pairs, compared with 5 percent for pairs formed a week apart (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:measurement}). For a person who dies in a hospital, it may be hours or days later. In-hospital deaths therefore never enter an hourly count. Between 15 and 20 percent of road-death certificates, depending on the group of states, the time of year, and the period, provide no clock time, and those deaths drop out of every count as well. % pretrends.rds, missing_hour: 15.4 to 20.1 percent by group, window and period.
In the treated states, an average summer window before abolition had 2,382 road deaths with a clock time, 110 of them in hour 0 (Table~\ref{tab:descriptives}).

The death registry is the standard source on mortality in Brazil, including in economics \citep[for example,][who measure homicide with it]{dixcarneiro2018economic}. Its coverage rests on a legal requirement: no burial may take place without a death record, which the registry office issues on the basis of a physician's death certificate where a physician is available \citep[art.~77]{brasil1973lei}. DST abolition did not change how deaths are recorded. In a triple difference like that of Section~\ref{sec:design}, neither the share of land-transport deaths that occur on the road (half of them) nor the share of road deaths without a clock time moves with abolition (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:records} and Table~\ref{tab:measurement}).

\subsection{Crashes on federal highways}

The Federal Highway Police (Pol\'icia Rodovi\'aria Federal, PRF) publishes every crash its officers respond to on federal highways, from 2007 to 2025, with date, clock time, municipality, numbers of people killed and injured, type of crash, and the light conditions as recorded by the officer: full daylight, dawn, dusk, or night \citep{prf2025dados}. We use two outcomes. Federal highway deaths count people killed at the crash scene \citep{prf2025anuario}, the same concept as road deaths in the SIM. Federal highway injury crashes are crashes with at least one casualty, a person killed or injured. Crashes without casualties are not used: an online self-report gradually replaced on-scene police response for them, at different dates in different states, which breaks that series differently in the two groups. The two sources overlap only in part. Road deaths cover every public road, urban streets included; federal highways run mostly outside urban areas, where the treated states had 1,176 deaths per summer before abolition, compared with 2,382 road deaths (Table~\ref{tab:descriptives}).

\subsection{Traffic flow}\label{sec:counts}

The National Traffic Count Plan (Plano Nacional de Contagem de Tr\'afego, PNCT) of the federal roads agency (DNIT) publishes hourly vehicle counts, by direction and vehicle class, at continuous counting stations on federal highways \citep{dnit2025pnct}. We use complete station-days counted from 2014 to May 2019 and from May 2021 to 2025, which cover the summers 2014/15 to 2018/19 and 2021/22 to 2024/25.\footnote{DNIT's contract for continuous counts ended in June 2019. The values published for the second half of 2019 were estimated with a statistical model, and there were no counts in 2020 \citep[p.~7]{dnit2020nota}. A new contract was tendered in 2020 \citep{dnit2020edital} and signed on December 30, 2020, and January 13, 2021; counting resumed in May 2021. We drop every station-day from June 2019 to December 2020, and any station-day whose daily total repeats exactly on the same weekday one to four weeks apart, which marks a modeled value.}

\subsection{Sun and clock}

For each municipal seat and day we compute sunrise and sunset in standard time from the solar position equations of \citet{noaa2025solar}, using the seat coordinates from IBGE and the standard offset of the municipality's legal time zone \citep{brasil1913decreto, brasil2008lei, brasil2013lei}. Every death and crash is then placed in a 60-minute bin of clock time relative to standard-time sunset or sunrise at its municipality on its date. Using NOAA's full solar algorithm \citep{meeus1998astronomical} instead moves sunset by at most 1.6 minutes and the main estimate from 29.2 to 29.8 log points (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:measurement}). The death certificates, the federal highway police records, and the traffic counts all give legal clock time, the time on the clock under whatever regime was in force. Section~\ref{sec:firststage} shows this in the officers' records, and Online Appendix~\ref{app:data} in the death certificates and the traffic counts.

\subsection{Sample}

The treated group consists of the 10 states that had DST every summer from 2008/09 to 2018/19 and the Federal District, which contains the capital, Bras\'ilia, and has the powers of a state. We refer to these 11 units as the treated states. The control group is the 12 states of the North and Northeast without DST in the sample: Rond\^onia, Roraima, Par\'a, Amap\'a, Maranh\~ao, Piau\'i, Cear\'a, Rio Grande do Norte, Para\'iba, Pernambuco, Alagoas, and Sergipe. We exclude Bahia and Tocantins, which had DST in one summer each, and Acre and Amazonas, which changed time zone during the sample (Figure~\ref{fig:map}). Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:bahia} uses Bahia's single summer with DST, 2011/12, as a check of sign. A season runs from July to June, so that each summer falls within one season, and is named by its first year. The sample runs from 2008/09, the first season under the 2008 decree, to 2023/24, the last for which the death registry is final, so it has 11 seasons with DST and 5 without.

The summer window runs from November 15 to February 14. Every day in it was under DST in every season before abolition: the latest start of DST in the sample was November 4, 2018, and the earliest end February 15, 2009. The same window is used in every season, before and after abolition, so no day in it is partly treated and the year-to-year variation in DST dates does not enter the comparison. The window starts at least 11 days after the latest start of DST and ends before the earliest end, so the weeks after clock changes, when the literature finds the effects of lost sleep \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight}, fall outside it. The off-season runs from April 1 to August 31, when no state ever had DST. The estimation panel has one row per state and day in these two windows: 23 states and 245 days in each of 16 seasons, or 90,160 state-days.

In the treated states, road deaths in hour 0 rose from 110 to 141 per summer after abolition, while those in the same hour of the off-season fell from 362 to 313; in the control states both fell. Taken together as a triple difference in logs, these changes amount to about 29 log points (33 percent). Pedestrian deaths in hour 0 of the treated states' summer doubled, from 13 to 27 per summer, while they fell in the off-season and in the control states.

\section{Empirical Strategy}\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Specification}

For each state $s$ and day $d$ in the summer window or the off-season, let $y_{sd}$ count the events that occur in one hour bin, hour 0 unless stated otherwise. The main specification is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main}
  y_{sd} = \exp\big(\beta\, T_s W_d A_d + \alpha_{s,w(d)} + \gamma_{s,t(d)} + \delta_d\big)\,\varepsilon_{sd},
\end{equation}
where $T_s$ marks the 11 treated states, $W_d$ days in the summer window, and $A_d$ seasons after abolition. The fixed effects are state by window ($\alpha$; summer window or off-season), state by season ($\gamma$) and date ($\delta$). We report $100\beta$, the effect in log points.

Each set of fixed effects removes a class of threats. State-by-window effects absorb every permanent difference between a state's summer and its off-season: tourism, the rainy season, and the fact that hour 0 falls at a later clock time in summer than in winter. State-by-season effects absorb anything that moves a state's counts proportionally in both windows of a season, such as its vehicle fleet, enforcement, or the pandemic. Date effects absorb national holidays and national shocks. The coefficient $\beta$ is then identified by the change, after abolition, in the gap between the summer and the off-season of the treated states, relative to the same change in the control states. The identifying assumption is that the gap would have moved in parallel in the two groups had DST not been abolished.

We estimate equation~(\ref{eq:main}) by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood, which requires only that the conditional mean be correct and handles the many zeros of a single hour's count \citep{santossilva2006log}: 88 percent of state-days have no road death in hour 0. The share of zeros implied by the fitted means matches the observed share within 1.1 percentage points in every outcome, and the ratio of the residual variance to the mean is between 0.9 and 1.6, so neither a zero-inflated nor a negative binomial model is needed. % inference.rds: zeros_obs_pct against zeros_poisson_pct, largest gap 1.05 (federal highway deaths, morning); dispersion 0.93 to 1.57.

We use a single hour as the outcome because, within the summer window alone, standard-time sunset differs across the municipalities of the sample by about two hours, so a fixed block of clock hours mixes hour 0 with hours whose light did not change and dilutes the effect. The definition of hour 0 also implies where an effect of light must appear and where it must not. A shock to the treated states' summers unrelated to light, such as a change in policing, has no reason to concentrate in the hour that follows standard-time sunset at each municipality on each date and to leave the hours on either side of it unaffected.

\subsection{Light or the clock: a dose of darkness}\label{sec:dose}

Interpreting the hour-0 estimate as the effect of light requires that no other post-2019 change systematically affected the clock times at which hour 0 occurs. In the treated states' summer it falls later on the clock than in their off-season (in S\~ao Paulo, about 7 p.m.\ in January and 5:30 p.m.\ in June) and later than in the control states, closer to the equator. A change after 2019 in the risk at that time of the evening, anywhere in the country, would therefore bias $\beta$. A second design separates light from clock time. For each municipal seat, date, and clock hour $h$, we compute from the solar position how dark the hour is without DST and how dark it was with it, counting a minute of night as 1, a minute of civil twilight (the sun less than six degrees below the horizon) as one half, and a minute of daylight as 0. The difference is the change in darkness abolition brought to that clock hour. It runs from 1, for an evening hour that went from full daylight to night, to $-1$, for a morning hour that went the other way, and it sums to zero over each day. Averaged over each state's municipal seats, weighted by their road deaths before abolition, it gives $D_{sdh}$, and the model is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dose}
  y_{sdh} = \exp\big(\theta_e\, X_{sdh}\, \mathbf{1}[h \ge 12] + \theta_m\, X_{sdh}\, \mathbf{1}[h < 12] + \alpha_{s,h,w(d)} + \gamma_{s,h,t(d)} + \delta_{h,d}\big)\,\varepsilon_{sdh},
\end{equation}
where $X_{sdh} = T_s W_d A_d D_{sdh}$, on a panel of states, days, and the 24 clock hours. Clock hours $h = 0, \dots, 23$ are split at noon into morning ($h < 12$) and evening ($h \ge 12$). The dose is non-zero only from 4 to 8 a.m.\ and from 5 to 10 p.m., so any cut between 8 a.m.\ and 5 p.m.\ gives the same split. Separate coefficients let the evening hours that turned dark and the morning hours that turned light have effects of different size, rather than forcing them to offset. % 23_light_dose.R dose: non-zero only at h = 4-7 (all negative) and h = 17-21 (all positive).
The clock-hour-by-date effects $\delta_{h,d}$ absorb any change in the risk at a given clock time on a given date anywhere in the country, so a change at particular times of the evening common to the whole country cannot drive $\theta_e$; Section~\ref{sec:dose-results} also removes changes specific to the treated states' clock hours. $\theta_e$ is the effect, in log points, of an evening clock hour going from full daylight to night, and $\theta_m$ that of a morning hour. Because every hour enters, with a dose of zero where the hour remained in full daylight or full darkness, the model also yields the net change in deaths over the day without selecting particular hours.

\subsection{Inference}

Standard errors are clustered by state. With 23 clusters, 11 of them treated, cluster-robust inference can over-reject \citep{cameron2008bootstrap}, so we report three further p-values. The first is from a score wild bootstrap of the Poisson model itself \citep{kline2012score}: the model is fitted with the null imposed, each state's score for the treatment term is multiplied by a random Webb weight, and the studentized score is compared with its distribution over 9,999 draws. The second is from a wild cluster bootstrap with the null imposed, Webb weights, and 9,999 draws \citep{webb2023reworking}, applied to the linear analogue of equation~(\ref{eq:main}) estimated by least squares on counts. The third is from permutation inference. In each draw, we assign the treatment to 11 of the 23 states at random and re-estimate the Poisson model. The p-value is the share of draws, counting the actual assignment, whose t-statistic is at least as large in absolute value as the actual one. The test compares t-statistics rather than estimates because states differ widely in size, and with heterogeneous clusters a test on the estimate can be unreliable while one on the t-statistic typically does better \citep{mackinnon2020randomization}. DST was not assigned at random, so the test asks whether an arbitrary group of 11 states would produce a t-statistic as large as that of the treated states.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

\subsection{The hour turned dark}\label{sec:firststage}

Panel B of Figure~\ref{fig:light} shows that hour 0 turned dark in the officers' records, and that the records use legal clock time. For crashes in the treated states' summer window, it plots the share recorded as occurring at dusk or at night by 10-minute bin of clock time relative to standard-time sunset. Under DST, that share reached one half at standard-time sunset; without DST, it reaches one half 50 minutes earlier. The curve moved by close to the hour the clock moved, which is what legal clock time implies. In hour 0 of the treated states, officers recorded 74 percent of crashes as occurring at dusk or at night before abolition, and a linear version of the triple difference of equation~(\ref{eq:main}) yields a rise of 23.6 percentage points (standard error 2.0) in that share. % light_dose.rds, first_stage: fs_pp, fs_se_pp, treated_pre_dark_pct.
The record is a coarse measure of light. Officers recorded many crashes in the last hour of sunlight as dusk, so the 24 points understate the change from sun above the horizon to sun below it. The dose of Section~\ref{sec:dose} measures darkness from the sun instead.

Panel A of Table~\ref{tab:main} reports the main estimates. In the hour that turned dark, road deaths rose by 29.2 log points (standard error 9.0), or 34 percent. Federal highway deaths rose by 53.9 log points (20.3) and federal highway injury crashes by 22.2 (5.6). The permutation p-values are 0.018, 0.014, and 0.007, the score bootstrap p-values 0.010, 0.023, and 0.001, and the wild bootstrap p-values on the linear model 0.010, 0.002, and 0.001. In the treated states, hour 0 had 110 road deaths per summer before abolition; after it, observed deaths exceed the counterfactual by 36 per summer in that hour alone, before any offset elsewhere in the day. % reallocation.rds, hours: eve+0 excess_per_season 35.6 (se 9.5).

Panel B reports the morning hour, which turned light. All three estimates are negative: $-3.3$ log points (12.4) for road deaths, $-11.3$ (20.4) for federal highway deaths, and $-14.2$ (8.3) for injury crashes. None is significant at the 5 percent level under clustered or permutation inference; the wild bootstrap on the linear model yields $p=0.031$ for federal highway deaths. The estimated reduction in morning road deaths is small and statistically indistinguishable from zero, unlike the evening increase, even though the two hours had similar pre-abolition death counts (107 and 110 per summer).

Figure~\ref{fig:hours} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) hour by hour around sunset and sunrise. In all three outcomes the estimate peaks at hour 0. For road deaths, the next hour, which went from twilight to night, also rises (16.4 log points, standard error 11.2). Of the other hours, only the second hour before sunrise, dark under both clocks, moves as much (26.4, 13.5). % sunset_design.rds, results: SIM, morning bin -2.
Federal highways show one more feature: crashes in the hour before sunset fall ($-22.3$ log points for injury crashes). Section~\ref{sec:trends} shows that this fall began in 2018/19, the last summer with DST, before abolition.

\subsection{Trends and robustness}\label{sec:trends}

Figure~\ref{fig:event-study} replaces the single post-abolition indicator with one coefficient per season, shown against the average season with DST, for hour 0 and the hour before it. For road deaths, the coefficients before abolition show no trend (a slope of $-0.5$ log points per season, standard error 2.1) and are jointly indistinguishable from each other ($p=0.18$). % pretrends.rds: pre_trend_lp, pre_trend_se, wald_pre_p.
All five seasons without DST lie above the average season with DST, the first two by the most. For federal highway injury crashes the earlier coefficients drift upward ($p<0.001$ for the joint test). In the hour before sunset, 2018/19 was already low relative to every earlier season, so the fall in that hour predates abolition. % switched_hour_event_study.rds: PRF injury crashes, hour -1, 2008/09-2017/18 between 24.9 and 55.5 log points against 2018/19.

Table~\ref{tab:robustness} reports checks for these trends and other threats. With a linear treated-by-summer trend fitted on all seasons, the estimate for road deaths is 39.9 log points (20.7). That trend also runs through the seasons after abolition and can absorb part of the effect. Panel B instead uses a Poisson version of the imputation estimator of \citet{borusyak2024revisiting}, which fits the counterfactual on untreated observations. With a trend learned before 2019 and extrapolated, road deaths rose 38 percent (95 percent interval $-12$ to 103), compared with 31 percent (7 to 54) without the trend. Extrapolating the trend costs precision, not effect. On federal highways the trend matters: with it, injury crashes rise by 5.6 log points (8.0) and by 8 percent ($-5$ to 26) in the imputation. We therefore rely on road deaths for the magnitude of the effect.

In the triple difference (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}, Panel A), the first two seasons without DST give 48.7 log points (11.6) and the last three 15.8 (10.3). The decline does not come from the summer window. Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:window-legs} splits the triple difference into its two legs, the gap between treated and control states in the summer window and the same gap in the off-season. In the summer window the gap rose with abolition and stayed up in all five seasons; estimated in the summer window alone, the effect is 39.3 (12.4) in the first two seasons and 31.2 (15.8) in the last three (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). The off-season leg moved instead: it was low in 2019/20, whose off-season includes the pandemic months of April to June 2020, and high in 2021/22 and 2022/23. Dropping every day from March 2020 to February 2022 gives 22.9 (9.1); the summer window alone, with no off-season comparison, gives 34.5 (13.4) over all five seasons. Across these ways of handling the pandemic and the off-season, the estimate lies between 22.9 and 34.5 log points.

Federal highways also had a shock of their own in the first summer without DST: a presidential order suspended the use of the PRF's stationary, mobile, and portable speed cameras from mid-August to December 23, 2019 \citep{brasil2019despacho, poder3602019radares}. Without that summer, the federal highway estimates are larger (65.0 for deaths and 25.7 for injury crashes), and the estimate for road deaths, which include deaths on federal highways, is smaller (22.7, standard error 9.8; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}).

Although control states did not change their clocks, activities scheduled according to Bras\'ilia time occurred one hour earlier by local clock time during DST. This difference disappeared after abolition. Their evening traffic did not move, but their road deaths in hour 0 rose relative to the rest of the day; to the extent that this rise came from those schedules, the triple difference understates the effect. Within the treated states alone, the same comparison of hour 0 with hours of the same day yields 47.2 (7.8) (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:within-group}).

Other comparisons in Panel C of Table~\ref{tab:robustness} leave the estimate in the same range: counting the control states' deaths at the clock time of the treated states' hour 0 on each date, so that both groups are compared at the same time of the evening (33.3, 12.1); state-by-day fixed effects that compare hour 0 with hours of the same state and day whose light did not change (27.7, 12.4; season by season in Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:within-day}); leaving out Carnival and the year-end holidays (30.8, 8.0); and leaving out the 279 coastal municipalities, the destinations of summer beach trips (36.3, 9.4; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). Treating the two hours after sunset as one bin lowers the estimate to 21.2 (8.0): the second hour changed less, and adding it dilutes the estimate. No single state or season is decisive: leaving out one state at a time gives between 24.3 and 34.1, and one season at a time between 22.7 and 35.2 (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:leave-out}). The control group matters more: with the eight states of the Northeast alone the estimate is 32.9 (9.2), with the four of the North alone 15.7 (8.8).

The sensitivity analysis of \citet{rambachan2023more} is less informative in this setting. Its target is the average post-abolition coefficient against 2018/19 (14.8 log points), not $\beta$, and with a single reference season that average is too imprecise to rule out small departures from a linear trend (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:honestdid}). % honestdid.rds: avg_post_lp 14.85; breakdown M 0.02.
The case for a causal reading rests on the pattern within the day: the peak in one hour defined by the local sun, the smaller changes in the neighboring hours, the absence of a rise at midday and at night, whose light did not change, and the concentration among pedestrians.

Recorded times heap on the hour and the half hour (34.5 and 23.0 percent of road deaths), so whether a death falls in hour 0 can depend on how its time was rounded. Shifting the hour 0 window by 5 to 15 minutes moves the estimate in the direction light predicts: it is larger when the window starts later and the hour is darker. Spreading each death recorded on the hour or half hour evenly over the 30 minutes around its recorded time gives 31.4 log points (9.5); dropping those deaths altogether leaves 16.7 (12.9), with less than half the sample (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:window-shift}). Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:measurement} collects these checks with those of Section~\ref{sec:data}: the match between death and crash times, the stability of the records across abolition, the extent of heaping, and the estimates with shifted windows or without rounded times.

\subsection{Light, not the clock}\label{sec:dose-results}

Table~\ref{tab:dose} reports equation~(\ref{eq:dose}). With an effect for every clock hour on every date, an evening clock hour that goes from full daylight to night has 47.7 log points (9.7) more road deaths. With date effects common to all hours instead, the estimate is about the same (45.7, 6.3), so changes after 2019 at particular clock times across the country do not drive it. The last row adds a separate effect for every clock hour in the treated states' summers after abolition, which absorbs any change specific to those states at a given clock time. The dose effect is then identified by differences in darkness at the same clock hour, which arise because the sun sets at different clock times across the treated states and across the dates of the summer, and it is 52.3 (18.4). For the same change in darkness, the morning coefficient is $-6.4$ (14.7), which differs from the evening's ($p<0.001$; permutation $p=0.001$). The baseline evening effect remains significant under the permutation test ($p=0.002$) and the score wild bootstrap ($p<0.001$). On federal highways, deaths respond too (79.5, 20.6), and injury crashes less (13.6, 9.0). Pedestrians respond most: a fully dark evening hour raises their road deaths by 115.8 log points (29.7), compared with 33.6 (11.9) for everyone else. % light_dose.rds: inference; dose (SIM pedestrian and non-pedestrian deaths, spec main).

\subsection{Is it sleep?}

Two features of the design keep acute sleep loss out of the estimates: abolition involved no lost night, and the summer window excludes the weeks after clock changes. A chronic effect through the clock time of sunset \citep{giuntella2019sunset} would run the other way, since an earlier clock sunset should lengthen sleep, not shorten it. And a sleep effect would not confine itself to one hour of the day. Panel D of Table~\ref{tab:robustness} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) for hours whose light did not change, midday and night. Nothing rises in them: road deaths move by $-4.5$ (5.8) and $-6.6$ (5.6) log points. The design can detect such changes: deaths from assault, examined the same way, jump in 2019/20 alone, over the whole day as well as in the early evening (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:assault}). Federal highway injury crashes fall at night ($-6.1$, $p=0.04$), consistent with the traffic that left the dark evening (Section~\ref{sec:traffic}).

\subsection{Who dies}

  \label{tab:pedestrians}

Inference as in Table~\ref{tab:main}, with the wild cluster bootstrap p-value from the linear model; in each permutation draw both members of the pair receive the same set of treated states, and the difference is divided by the square root of the sum of the two squared standard errors. The increase falls disproportionately on pedestrians (Table~\ref{tab:pedestrians}). Pedestrian road deaths in hour 0 rose by 76.6 log points (29.8), more than doubling, while the deaths of all other road users rose by 17.9 (7.8). Pedestrians were 11.7 percent of road deaths in hour 0 before abolition and account for 43.4 percent of the excess after it (standard error 10.3). On federal highways the contrast is sharper: 170 log points for pedestrian deaths and 26 for all others. The pedestrian estimates are significant under the wild bootstrap and the permutation test in all three outcomes. The difference between pedestrians and others is significant on federal highways (permutation $p=0.001$ for deaths and for injury crashes) and borderline for road deaths ($p=0.075$). The federal highway contrast does not come from their trend: with a pre-abolition trend extrapolated, pedestrian deaths there rise by 103.9 log points (34.3) and other deaths by 15.3 (23.5). % mechanism.rds, trend: extrap_lp for PRF pedestrian and non-pedestrian deaths.

Among the other road users (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:road-users}), motorcyclist deaths rose by 19.6 log points (10.9), and the estimate for car occupants is zero but imprecise ($-0.2$, standard error 35.2); deaths in the residual group, 85 percent of them with no type of vehicle recorded, rose by 55.8 (26.4). The ordering among pedestrians, motorcyclists, and car occupants is the one visibility predicts. A pedestrian is the road user who most depends on being seen, and pedestrian crash risk is the most sensitive to ambient light around the clock changes \citep{sullivan2002role}; pedestrian deaths at night also fall on brighter moonlit nights \citep{tyndall2025road}. The pattern is also hard to reconcile with sleep, which would impair drivers whoever they hit. The increase was larger on weekends and holidays (41.3, 15.8) than on weekdays (16.1, 10.0), and remains so when Carnival and the year-end holidays are excluded (39.3, 16.2), so it is not confined to the commute home. Street lighting points the same way, though imprecisely. When the municipalities of each state are split at the median share of households on unlit streets, the estimate is 42.5 log points (10.0) in municipalities above the median and 10.9 (16.0) in those below it ($p=0.10$ for the difference; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:lighting}). Among men, about four fifths of the dead, road deaths rose by 33.8 log points (9.9) and federal highway deaths by 65.2 (20.7); for women the estimates are too imprecise to compare (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sex-age}).

\subsection{Traffic followed the light}\label{sec:traffic}

Drivers adapted to the new light. Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:volume} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) on hourly vehicle counts at federal highway stations. After abolition, traffic in the treated states' summer fell by 6.4 log points (2.2) in hour 0 and by 5.1 (1.3) in the hour before it, and rose by 11.7 (5.0) in the morning hour that turned light, with permutation p-values of 0.069, 0.025, and 0.159. None of the stations counted after abolition had been counted before it: counting resumed in 2021 under a new contract, at new stations (Section~\ref{sec:counts}). On the 30 stations that were moved at most 2 kilometers along the same highway, the evening fall is smaller and not significant ($-3.1$, 3.1) and the morning rise larger (18.7, 5.1).

Subtracting the volume estimate from the crash estimate gives the change in crashes per vehicle. For a like-for-like comparison, the crash estimates in that table come from the summers covered by the traffic counts, 2014/15 to 2018/19 and 2021/22 to 2024/25, over which federal highway injury crashes in hour 0 show no trend before abolition ($-2.8$ log points per season, standard error 2.9). % traffic_volume.rds, risk: pre_trend_lp, PRF injury accidents, eve+0.
On those summers, injury crashes in hour 0 rose by 17.6 log points (7.5), and injury crashes per vehicle by 24.0 ($p=0.005$), more than crashes themselves; in the morning hour that turned light, crashes per vehicle fell by 28.1 ($p=0.083$). Fewer vehicles travel in hour 0, and each faces a higher risk. The stations cover federal highways only and say nothing about urban traffic, where many of the pedestrian deaths in the death registry occur.

\subsection{The morning hour does not offset the evening hour}\label{sec:offset}

\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:excess} turns the estimates into events per summer: observed counts in the treated states' summers after abolition minus those predicted without it. Panel A sums every clock hour of the day, weighted by how much its light changed (equation~\ref{eq:dose}). Abolition added 62 road deaths per summer window (standard error 12; permutation $p=0.001$): 57 in the evening hours that grew darker, and 5 in the morning hours that grew lighter, where the effect is indistinguishable from zero. Extended to a full DST season under the 2017 rule, about 108 days instead of the 92 of the window, the estimate yields 74 additional deaths (standard error 14). This extension applies coefficients estimated within the summer window to days outside it. The count requires no selection of particular hours, but it assumes that hours with no change in the modeled darkness dose were unaffected. A dose of zero does not mean that the light did not change at all: the hour before standard-time sunset stayed in daylight, with the sun lower. Panel D of Table~\ref{tab:robustness} finds no detectable change at midday or at night, but with about 580 road deaths a summer in each, its confidence intervals also include a fall as large as the net count. % placebo_hours.rds: 585 and 572 per season; 95 percent intervals about -86 to +42 and -93 to +26 deaths.

Panel B adds up hours estimated one at a time, without that structure. The two evening hours that turned darker added 57 road deaths per summer (standard error 19), and the morning hour that turned light removed 3 (11). That hour gained traffic along with light: on federal highways its vehicles rose by about 12 percent and its injury crashes per vehicle fell by 28 log points (Section~\ref{sec:traffic}), so a lower risk per trip was spread over more trips. Together, these three hours added a net 54 deaths (20), 17 percent of the deaths predicted in them ($p=0.007$). % reallocation.rds, sums: 54.23, se 20.06, pct_of_cf 17.3, p 0.0069.
Hours $-1$ to $+1$ at each end, from one hour before to two hours after sunset and sunrise, give 53 (35), and all seven hours 41 (41). Estimated directly, the whole day gives $-5$ deaths (66). Estimating the effect over the entire day introduces variation from hours in which the effect is small or absent, making the net estimate considerably less precise than the evening-hour estimate. The whole-day count can therefore neither confirm the net figure nor rule it out, and we do not read it as evidence that abolition only moved deaths between hours of the day. On federal highways, the dose model implies 31 deaths (12; permutation $p=0.135$) per summer; injury crashes, whose response to darkness is weaker, net 43 (57).

In levels, a clock hour that goes from full daylight to night has about 61 percent more road deaths, and more than three times as many pedestrian deaths. That pedestrians bear so much of the increase matches evidence that their crash risk in the dark is up to seven times that in daylight \citep{sullivan2002role}. The effect on all road users is larger than projections for the United States. Over the three hours of Panel B, abolition added 17 percent to the predicted road deaths, while \citet{coate2004effects} project that year-round DST would lower deaths in the morning and evening periods it affects by 13 percent for pedestrians and 3 percent for vehicle occupants. Part of the gap may reflect who is on the road: before abolition, pedestrians and motorcyclists were 35 percent of road deaths in hour 0 of the treated states' summer, and motorcyclist deaths rose with abolition, by less than pedestrian deaths and by more than those of car occupants. % road_users.rds: pre_per_season pedestrian 12.8 + motorcyclist 25.5 of 109.9.

\subsection{Before and after travel adjusted}\label{sec:transitions}

Abolition measures the effect of a darker evening after five summers in which people could change when they travel. The clock changes before 2019 measure the same change of light before travel had time to adjust. When the clocks went back each February, the evening hour 0 went from daylight to dark overnight, while work, school, and travel kept to the same clock hours; when they went forward each spring, the reverse. Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:transitions} compares hour 0 in the three weeks after each change with the three weeks before, in the treated relative to the control states, and uses the same calendar days of the seasons after abolition, when no clock moved, to net out the seasonal change. In the three weeks after the clocks went back, road deaths in hour 0 rose by 54.6 log points (21.9); after they went forward, deaths fell by 29.9 (18.5). Read as the effect of a darker evening, the two average 42.3 (13.8), compared with 29.2 after abolition. Each change also adds or removes an hour of sleep, which acts on every hour of the day and pushes both transition estimates toward zero; compared with hours of the same day, which nets it out, the transitions give 79.1 (14.2) and abolition 27.7 (12.4). In one model that allows for the overlap of the two samples, abolition minus the clock changes is $-13.1$ (12.5) in the first comparison and $-51.4$ (18.3) in the second. Only the within-day comparison, which absorbs day-level shocks common to all hours, including those associated with sleep, yields a statistically significant difference between the transition and abolition estimates. The two settings also differ in the time of year, and the effect of abolition is not the same across the summer window (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window-parts}). From November 15 to December 7, while schools are in session, abolition raised road deaths in hour 0 by 58.1 log points (12.6). From December 24 to January 15 it is $-12.3$ (16.8). From January 16 to 31 it is 49.1 (15.6), although schools are still on break then in every treated state but Goi\'as \citep{saopaulo2018resolucao, goias2018parecer, minas2023ano}. The school calendar alone therefore cannot explain how the estimate varies across the summer window: no increase is detectable from Christmas to mid-January, while the late-January school break shows about as large an effect as the school weeks. The three weeks after each clock change fall while schools are in session, the same part of the school year as the weeks from mid-November to early December. Compared with abolition in those weeks, the clock changes are not distinguishable from it: the difference is 15.8 (18.0) in hour 0 and $-22.2$ (20.9) in the comparison with hours of the same day (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:transitions}). The gap over the whole window thus points mainly to the weeks from Christmas to mid-January rather than to a uniformly smaller effect after travel adjusted. In the school weeks, the effect of a darker evening after five summers is close to its effect in the weeks after a clock change, though the intervals leave room for a moderate decline. Late January gives an estimate of about the same size. The gap between those weeks and the school weeks changes little without the coastal municipalities or without Par\'a, a control state whose 2019 school year ran from March 2019 to January 2020 \citep{para2018calendario}, and before abolition the parts of the window moved alike (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window-parts}). Traffic on federal highways shows no detectable difference between the two periods. Vehicles in hour 0 fell by 7.4 log points from December 24 to January 15 and by 5.3 in the school weeks, a difference of 2.1 (standard error 2.4), and the same holds for trucks and buses in that hour and for the day's traffic (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:traffic-parts}). These checks do not rule out holiday travel on other roads as an explanation, and the data do not say why no increase is detectable in those weeks. On federal highways the same comparison implies 121 log points for deaths at the clock changes and 54 after abolition, and about the same for injury crashes (20.6 and 22.2).

\section{What Abolition Cost}\label{sec:cost}

  \label{tab:cost}

Column 1 is the estimate. Column 2 adds road deaths without a clock time, assuming they occur in the affected hours in the same proportion as deaths with one. Column 3 adds deaths off the road, 85 percent of them in hospitals, under the same assumption; it is an extrapolation. The share is of all land-transport deaths in the treated states' summer window before abolition. The whole-season count applies coefficients estimated in the summer window to the additional days covered by the 2017 DST rule. Panel B: the summer-window counts valued at the value of a statistical life (VSL) by the reference approach of \citet{robinson2019valuing} and two alternatives, from gross national income per head at purchasing-power parity in 2025, in international dollars; and the Ipea social cost of a death on a federal highway, a human-capital cost that excludes the value of life itself (December 2014 prices adjusted to December 2025 prices using the IPCA and converted at the 2025 PPP rate of 2.554 reais per international dollar). Table~\ref{tab:cost} scales and values the net count of the dose model. Column 1 reports the estimated increase in road deaths with a recorded time: 62 deaths per summer window and 74 when extended to the full DST season (Table~\ref{tab:excess}). Both counts assume, as discussed in Section~\ref{sec:offset}, that hours with no change in the modeled darkness dose were unaffected. The full season is the relevant unit for the policy comparison, since reinstating DST would restore all of it. The figure of 74 deaths is obtained by applying the average effect of the summer window to the extra days, in early November and mid-February; that average includes the weeks from Christmas to mid-January, when no increase was detectable (Section~\ref{sec:transitions}). Refitting the dose model with a separate effect for each part of the window and applying the effect of November 15 to December 7 to the extra days yields 79 deaths (Table~\ref{tab:excess}). Early November falls in the same part of the school year as November 15 to December 7; mid-February, when many school systems are reopening, may be closer to the smaller estimate for February 1 to 14. Because the extra days lie outside the estimation window, 79 is a sensitivity calculation. % light_dose.rds, dose: season_net_term 78.8 (SIM, main).
 The summer-window deaths are 1.0 percent of all land-transport deaths in the treated states' summer window. Column 2 assumes that road deaths without a recorded time fall in the affected hours in the same proportion as those with one, which gives 77 per summer window. Column 3 further assumes that deaths occurring off the road, 85 percent of them in hospitals, follow the same hourly pattern as deaths at the crash scene, yielding 157 deaths per summer window. This is an extrapolation: the design cannot identify the crash hour for in-hospital deaths. The resulting bias could run in either direction, because pedestrians struck in darkness may be more or less likely than other crash victims to die at the crash scene.

We value a death with the reference rule of \citet{robinson2019valuing} for transferring a value of a statistical life (VSL) to a lower-income country: the US ratio of VSL to income per head, 160, extrapolated to Brazil with an income elasticity of 1.5, so that $\mathit{VSL}_{\mathit{BR}} = 160\, Y_{\mathit{US}}\, (Y_{\mathit{BR}}/Y_{\mathit{US}})^{1.5}$, where $Y$ is gross national income per head at purchasing power parity in 2025 \citep{worldbank2026wdi}. The resulting VSL is 1.8 million international dollars, or R\$4.7 million at the 2025 parity rate (Online Appendix~\ref{app:cost} gives the inputs and the alternative rules). We report every value in 2025 international dollars, a unit with the purchasing power that a US dollar has in the United States; reais are converted at the purchasing-power-parity rate, not at the exchange rate. % total_cost.rds, vsl: 1,825,618 international dollars; R$ 4.66338 million.
At that value, the deaths in one summer window have an estimated cost of 114 million international dollars (standard error 22), rising to 287 million under the broadest scaling; over a whole season of DST, the deaths in column 1 cost 135 million. The two alternative rules of \citet{robinson2019valuing} give larger values, up to 571 million per summer window. A human-capital valuation of a death on a federal highway \citep{ipea2015acidentes}, which leaves out the value of life itself, gives 19 to 49 million. The valuation leaves out two costs. Nonfatal injuries rose too, as the federal highway injury crashes show, but the death registry has no counterpart for them, and the federal highway estimate is sensitive to its trend. Nor does it include the cost of avoidance: traffic in the hour that turned dark fell, consistent with trips moved or forgone, but the data do not show who changed their travel or at what cost. The deaths are the harm that remained after that avoidance.
% total_cost.rds, value: DST season, count A, rule (a): 134.7 (se 26.3).

The energy side of the ledger has changed sign over time. The technical note behind the 2019 decision estimated that DST had raised electricity load by about 0.7 percent \citep{mme2019nota}; on that estimate, abolition saved a little electricity at the price of the deaths in the darkened evenings. For today's system, the grid operator estimates that reinstating DST would save 96 to 139 million international dollars in thermal-generation fuel in one summer and, by lowering the evening peak by about 2 GW, about 0.7 billion a year in payments for reserve capacity \citep{ons2024nota}. These are projections of system costs, not measures of welfare: the fuel savings cover October 2024 to February 2025, and the capacity payments are annual and rest on the prices of the 2021 capacity auction. The fuel savings are of the same order as the value of the deaths of a DST season in column 1 of Table~\ref{tab:cost}. Reinstating DST would also restore the two clock changes a year that abolition removed, whose cost the literature attributes to lost sleep in the days after the spring change: more road crashes \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight} and, in Brazil, more deaths from heart attacks \citep{toro2015daylight}. Section~\ref{sec:transitions} compares the clock changes with abolition, but the summer window excludes those weeks, and the valuation here does not include them.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

When Brazil stopped moving its clocks, the evening hour that lost its sunlight became deadlier on the road, disproportionately for pedestrians, and the morning hour that gained light did not become detectably safer. The deaths followed the local sun, not the clock. When only deaths at the crash scene with a recorded time are counted, and hours that remained in full daylight or full darkness are assumed unaffected, abolition of DST added 62 road deaths from mid-November to mid-February each year, and about 74 if the effect is extended to the rest of the season. In the weeks when schools were in session, the effect of abolition over the five summers without DST was close to the effect at the clock changes, when the light moved overnight and travel had no time to adjust; across the summer, the increase was not detectable from Christmas to mid-January but was detectable in late January, when most treated states were still on school break.

The estimates have limits that matter for their use. They count only deaths at the crash scene with a recorded time, not deaths off the road or without a recorded time, nor nonfatal injuries. The sample has 23 states and five summers without DST, two of them in the pandemic; the estimate lies between 23 and 34 log points across the ways of handling the pandemic and the off-season, and in the summer comparison it shows no clear decline over the five seasons. The net count over the day assumes that hours with no change in the modeled darkness dose were unaffected; estimated without that restriction, the whole-day effect is too imprecise to say whether some deaths moved to other hours. Federal highway records are sensitive to a pre-existing trend, and the traffic counts cover only federal highways.

For Brazil, the estimates speak to the choice between reinstating seasonal DST and maintaining year-round standard time. Section~\ref{sec:cost} compares the estimated mortality costs with the projected energy consequences. The estimates are less directly transferable to other settings. In summer, seasonal and permanent DST set the same clock, so the estimates are the cost, in summer evenings, of choosing permanent standard time over either. They say nothing about winter, when permanent DST would darken the mornings, and they are least informative at latitudes higher than Brazil's. Nor do they weigh the clock changes, energy use, or the effects of the clock on sleep. Part of what people did to protect themselves, driving less in the hour that turned dark, is already in the estimates. Within these limits, the evening hour that lost its light became deadlier on the road, deaths in the morning hour that gained it did not detectably decline, and a disproportionate share of the lives lost are pedestrians, whom street lighting and road design can protect when the clock does not.
